mcqs.question:
A
Save
has an onclick handler. What is still missing for keyboard and screen-reader users?
options: Nothing: the role makes it a real button for assistive technology.
It is not focusable and does not activate with Enter or Space; that behavior must be added by hand, or the div replaced with a native <button>.
Only an aria-label that describes the action.
Only CSS that makes it look pressed when clicked.
mcqs.explanation: The role changes only the accessibility-tree mapping; it adds no behavior, so the control has no tab stop and no Enter or Space activation. A native <button> supplies keyboard activation, focusability, and its role for free, which is why native HTML is the default. The strongest distractor is option 0: it reflects the common belief that ARIA roles bring the element's behavior with them, when in fact users get a control they can hear but cannot operate.

mcqs.question: Which of these gives a text input a durable accessible name?
options: placeholder="Email address"
title="Email address"
<label for="email">Email address</label> paired with <input id="email">
Wrapping the input in a div whose text reads Email address
mcqs.explanation: An explicitly associated label gives the control a stable name that persists while typing, enlarges the clickable target, and is the label-association technique WCAG documents. The strongest distractor is option 0: a placeholder is a hint that disappears on input and was never an identifying name. Option 1 is only a last-resort name that is not reliably exposed to all assistive technology, and option 3 is text that is never associated with the control at all.

mcqs.question: aria-hidden="true" is set on a container that includes a button that is still focusable. What do keyboard screen-reader users experience?
options: The button is removed from the tab order along with the accessibility tree
The button is still in the tab order but is exposed with no name or role: a silent tab stop
The container is hidden from the accessibility tree, but the button inside keeps its name and role
The button disappears visually as well
mcqs.explanation: aria-hidden removes content from the accessibility tree but does not remove focusability, so a focusable element inside a hidden subtree stays keyboard-reachable while announcing nothing; MDN documents hiding focused or focusable elements this way as an anti-pattern (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-hidden). The fix is to keep the control outside the hidden subtree or hide it with hidden or display: none, which removes it from the tab order too. The strongest distractor is option 2: the button is inside the hidden subtree, so its name and role are stripped along with the container.

mcqs.question: What does tabindex="-1" do?
options: Removes the element from all focus, including programmatic focus
Adds the element to the tab order before all other controls
Makes the element programmatically focusable, for example with focus() after a route change, without adding it to the sequential tab order
Behaves exactly like tabindex="0"
mcqs.explanation: A value of negative one permits programmatic focus without adding a tab stop, which is the standard tool for moving focus to a heading or main region after a route change or dialog interaction. Zero adds the element to the natural order, and positive values create a separate order that is hard to maintain and confusing for users. The strongest distractor is option 1: it swaps the meaning of negative and positive values, the most common tabindex mix-up.

mcqs.question:
Saved.

gets its text replaced after a user action. What announcement behavior does role="status" imply?
options: None: live behavior requires an explicit aria-live attribute
aria-live="off" by default, like the attribute's own default
aria-live="polite" by default: updates are announced without interrupting the user
aria-live="assertive" by default: updates interrupt immediately
mcqs.explanation: The status role carries an implicit aria-live="polite" (with aria-atomic="true"), so concise status updates are announced at the next opportunity rather than interrupting what the user is reading (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Live_regions). The strongest distractor is option 1: it is true that the aria-live attribute's own default is off, but the role brings its own implicit value, which is why writing the explicit attribute alongside is often redundant.

mcqs.question: An automated accessibility audit reports zero violations. What can you conclude?
options: The page conforms to WCAG 2.2 AA
Only that the automated rules passed; keyboard operation, reading order, alt-text quality, and real assistive-technology behavior still need manual testing
Manual testing is only needed for pages with custom ARIA widgets
Keyboard testing is unnecessary because the scan covers focus order
mcqs.explanation: Automated checks are useful for repeatable rules, but most criteria require human judgment: whether the alt text conveys the right meaning, whether focus and reading order make sense, and how the page behaves with a real screen reader. The strongest distractor is option 2: native-HTML pages still need manual passes, because reading order, heading structure, and text quality are not ARIA-specific problems.

scenarios.prompt: This toggle control is about to ship in a design system. Identify every accessibility failure in the markup and script, then describe the implementation you would ship instead.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The control fails on every axis at once. It has no role, so assistive technology exposes a generic container; no accessible name, so nothing identifies what it does; no state exposure, because the on/off condition lives only in a CSS class rather than an attribute assistive technology can read; no focusability, because a div without tabindex is not in the tab order; and no keyboard activation, because only onclick is wired, so pointer users alone can operate it. The first fix is to question the markup: a native input type="checkbox" with an associated label already provides role, name, state, keyboard activation, and focus, and can be styled as a switch. If the product truly requires custom markup, the minimum contract is: a button element (or role="switch") so the role is real; a programmatically determinable name from visible text or aria-labelledby; aria-checked kept in sync on every activation path, not a CSS class; Enter and Space activation matching pointer activation; a sensible place in the tab order; and a visible :focus-visible indicator. Finally, verify name, role, and state with an accessibility inspector and a real screen reader rather than trusting the visual design.
rubric: Identifies all five failures: no role, no name, no programmatic state, not focusable, no keyboard activation.
Reaches first for native HTML (input type="checkbox" plus label) and can style it as a switch, instead of defaulting to custom ARIA.
If custom: knows aria-checked must be updated on every activation path and that CSS classes carry no semantics.
Requires Enter and Space activation plus a visible :focus-visible treatment.
Verifies the result with an accessibility inspector and a real screen reader, not just visually.

scenarios.prompt: This client-side router swaps the view but does nothing else, and keyboard and screen-reader users report that the page 'changes silently'. Design the focus and announcement behavior for route changes, and explain where the logic should live.
scenarios.modelAnswer: A client-rendered route change must do three things deliberately. First, update the document title so the page identity changes for assistive technology and history entries. Second, provide a clear focus destination in the new view: give the new content's primary heading (or the main region) tabindex="-1" and call focus() on it, which moves focus programmatically without inserting a permanent tab stop; this also guarantees focus does not remain on a control that just disappeared. Third, keep normal link semantics and browser history behavior so back, forward, and deep links work, and make sure the new content carries correct headings, landmarks, names, and states. Do not add a generic aria-live 'page loaded' announcement: the title change plus the focused heading is the established, richer signal, and an extra live channel mostly adds noise; announce only what is useful. The implementation belongs in the routing or accessibility platform layer, written once, not repeated per page. Finally, test back and forward navigation, deep links, loading and error states, keyboard traversal, and screen-reader reading order.
rubric: Updates the document title on every route change and can say why it matters.
Moves focus to the new heading or main region using tabindex="-1" and knows why -1 rather than 0.
Rejects a generic aria-live announcement in favor of title plus focus destination, with reasoning.
Places the behavior once in the routing or platform layer instead of duplicating it per page.
Includes testing for back and forward navigation, deep links, and error states with keyboard and a screen reader.
